title: Pauli Encodings & Unclonable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Sébastien Designolle, Omar Fawzi
abstract: The unclonable bit question asks whether quantum encryption can prevent an adversary from producing two systems that both reveal the plaintext once the key is disclosed. We introduce and study Pauli Encodings, a simple class of one-bit encryption schemes whose ciphertexts are normalized eigenspace projectors of Pauli strings. For every Pauli Encoding with K Pauli strings, we prove a universal lower bound $1/2+1/(2\sqrt{K})$ on the optimal monogamy-of-entanglement winning probability, together with sharper bounds for several structured families. We then establish two limitations of natural approaches to unclonable security. First, if the Pauli strings are restricted to strings of X and Z of length n, the encoding is not secure. Second, we identify a universal 3/4 obstruction showing that arguments based only on pairwise guessing marginals cannot establish unclonable-indistinguishable security. When the Pauli strings all pairwise anticommute, the protocol becomes the one studied in [Quantum 10, 2157 (2026)]. We exploit the symmetry of this protocol to solve the third level of the natural semidefinite programming relaxation obtaining an asymptotic upper bound of approximately 0.5556 on the winning probability. Finally, we prove strong unclonable-indistinguishable security against bounded-local-dimension adversaries and strong indistinguishability security for several efficient Pauli families. First-level NPA computations provide additional numerical evidence towards the strong unclonable-indistinguishable security.
summary: This paper analyzes the security of Pauli Encoding schemes designed for unclonable encryption by studying the associated cloning game. Using advanced mathematical tools like moment matrix hierarchies and representation theory, the authors derive tight lower and upper bounds on the adversary's winning probability. The work provides strong theoretical constraints on what quantum cryptography can achieve in preventing state cloning.
main_problem: The paper investigates the security of quantum encryption schemes against an adversary attempting to clone or distinguish encrypted states, addressing the Unclonable Bit Question.
main_result: It establishes universal lower bounds on the winning probability for Pauli Encodings and derives strong upper bounds (e.g., $\le 0.5556$) using advanced SDP relaxations for specific families of encodings.
method: The authors employ techniques from quantum information theory, including analyzing the monogamy-of-entanglement game and utilizing moment matrix hierarchies (NPA) combined with representation theory to derive rigorous bounds.
model_or_system: The core model is Pauli Encodings, where ciphertexts are normalized eigenspace projectors of Pauli strings acting on a quantum system. The analysis involves studying the security against adversaries in cloning games.
key_observables: Monogamy-of-Entanglement (MoE) winning probability ($P_{	ext{win MoE}}$), optimal cloning probability ($P^*_{	ext{win cloning}}$), and derived block matrices $B(K)_{\lambda,\epsilon}(g)$.
important_parameters: The number of Pauli strings ($K$), the system dimension ($2^n$), and the level of the moment relaxation (e.g., Level One, Two, Three).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on establishing equivalences between positive semidefiniteness of moment matrices and derived block matrices, and assumes certain structures for Pauli string families.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the security problem (Unclonable Bit Question) using Pauli Encodings, deriving general lower bounds, establishing no-go results via pairwise marginals, and finally applying advanced moment/representation theory techniques (NPA hierarchy) to derive tight upper bounds.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of representation theory (symmetric group characters, Specht modules) to bound quantum information security parameters is highly relevant for theoretical physicists working on fundamental limits in quantum communication.
